- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

4	package-defaults table, and the rule that a budget moves the pace and never the standard. It sits in
5	the base skill's own package, beside `SKILL.md`. Open it when a setting is being resolved, proposed,
6	or recorded, and not before. Every rule below reads exactly as it read in the rulebook body.
7	
8	How the pack behaves is a **named setting** living in one of four nested scopes, and a setting belongs to
9	the scope it describes. Broader values are inherited downward until a narrower scope overrides them on
10	the human's word. Resolution reads from the narrowest scope out — **session beats host beats personal beats
11	package default** (SPEC E-13):
12	
13	| Scope | Home | Holds settings about |
14	|---|---|---|
15	| package defaults | the table below, in this file | the pack out of the box |
16	| personal profile | `~/.claude/live-spec/profile.md` | the person — follows them across every project |
17	| host profile | `<host>/.live-spec/profile.md` | this one project |
18	| session | the human's live word, held only in the conversation itself | the conversation running right now |
19	
20	An override exists only as a written line in its profile file. Setting one leaves a dated journal note
21	in the home it governs, keeping every divergence visible (SPEC INV-14). The session scope is the one exception.
22	It lives only in the human's spoken word and dies with the conversation. The agent never writes it
23	anywhere on its own. Making it outlive the session is a promotion into the profile it describes, on
24	the human's word, journaled like any other override. Proactivity mode and trust are written
25	only on the human's word, and the agent may propose but never set them (SPEC INV-9). Profiles are re-read at the same
26	freshness points as skills (rule 8). A profile line the current pack does not recognize is ignored out
27	loud, named once in the session's next report as a visible, ordinary skip, never an error.
28	
29	**The profile is found or founded at setup (SPEC B-3)**. The pack looks for the personal profile before
30	the founding questions resolve. It looks at founding, at adoption's orient, and at the first session on
31	a new machine or with a new human. Found ⇒ loaded and said aloud. Absent ⇒ an offer to create it from
32	`templates/profile.template.md`, which sits in the pack's own tree. The human tells about themselves and
33	may name sources for the pack to read and propose from. Every line lands on the human's word, and a declined proposal is dropped (INV-9
34	caps it: mode and trust move only on their word). A declined step runs the session on package
35	defaults, said aloud, and the offer returns at the next setup. A worker session never onboards
36	anyone, since its brief carries its setting lines (SPEC ACT-3).
37	
38	The personal layer has one home, the profile. The machine-global instruction file (for example
39	`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) is a thin loader. It carries the pointer that loads the profile, plus only the
40	bootstrap lines that must hold before
41	any pack file is read. It is those bootstrap lines' one home, and the profile never restates them (SPEC E-16).
42	
43	### Package defaults
44	
45	| Setting | Default | A profile may say | Card |
46	|---|---|---|---|
47	| `language.docs` | English — docs, commits, code, artifacts | another docs language | visible |
48	| `language.chat` | mirror the human's language | pin one (e.g. Russian) | visible |
49	| `proactivity.mode` | ask-at-max — surface forks, wait on taste calls | max-proactive: proceed on recommendations, batch questions | visible |
50	| `trust` | low — human word before outward moves | raised only by the human (INV-9) | internal |
51	| `prover.cadence` | FULL pass before every MINOR bump; CROSS-LINK on every surface add | tighter (e.g. live-spec itself: before every push) or looser, recorded | internal |
52	| `worker.tiering` | router proposes the cheapest sufficient tier; senior may override, logged | fixed tier per size class (SPEC D-2) | internal |
53	| `checkpoints.home` | `<host>/.live-spec/checkpoints/`, gitignored | another host path | internal |
54	| `spec.file` | `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` — the host's product spec file; every pack guide reads "PRODUCT_SPEC.md" as this file under its recorded name | a host that adopted under its own name keeps it, recorded as one host-profile line (e.g. `spec.file: SPEC.md`); a rename may be offered together with its pointer sweep, never forced (SPEC INV-90) | internal |
55	| `work-kind.host-default` | none — each wish's kind is called at intake | a host with one usual kind names it as the intake default (SPEC T-16) | internal |
56	| `project.kind` | none — asked at founding and at adoption's orient, always the human's answer, never profile-seeded or inferred (SPEC INV-36) | the host's own kind: book · backend service · static site · fullstack app · CLI · skill pack · a custom kind through the queue; seeds project-wide defaults, never overriding an explicit line; updated on the human's word the moment the project outgrows it, journaled | visible |
57	| `project.layers` | none — declared at founding beside `project.kind`, naming this kind's concrete footprint categories (SPEC INV-135) | this project's own categories, one line: a codebase's frontend/backend/store, a photo site's content/rendering-engine/deployment, a campaign's message/channels/assets; the per-kind footprint-and-proof table in `ARCHITECTURE.md` is the scaffold each founding fills | internal |
58	| `project.proofs` | none — declared at founding beside `project.kind`, naming this kind's concrete test-ladder rungs (SPEC INV-135) | this project's own rungs, one line: tests and rendered checks, a byte-diff and an eye-walk, a register lint and the owner's review; a `project.kind` recorded with neither layers nor proofs is incomplete | internal |
59	| `project.design-principles` | none for a kind with no visual surface; a visual kind (e.g. frontend / fullstack app) declares its set at founding, seeded from that kind's starter table in `ARCHITECTURE.md`'s per-kind design-principles section (SPEC INV-136) | the project's own checkable design rules, one line, extended past the starter set through the queue; a visual kind recorded with none is flagged the way a kind recorded with no layers or proofs is (SPEC INV-135) | internal |
60	| `design-sync` | off — a host with visual components may switch it on (recorded profile line, SPEC E-18, INV-14) | on: a landing's declared components sync to the team's design project, every sync behind the human's publish gate (rule 17) | internal |
61	| `feedback-upstream` | off — the outbound feedback arm is silent; a host switches it on with a recorded profile line (SPEC INV-161, INV-14) | on: on a rare strong reaction the pack offers, with the human's explicit yes, to draft a private upstream note to the pack's authors into `outbox/`; never sends, delivery the human's own step | internal |
62	| `lanes.cap` | 3 — up to three build lanes roll at once without asking (SPEC T-18, INV-214) | a leaner plan lowers it, a richer one raises it, recorded with the plan it fits; the owner's 2026-07-06 value of three lives in his profile | internal |
63	| `budget.pressure` | full — every check runs at full strength; the economy ladder's rung (SPEC T-19, INV-40); a rung moves the pace and never the standard, stated under this table | lean or tight, only on the human's word (a session's word or a profile line; asked — or the default told — at a project's setup, founding or adoption, alongside `project.kind`; the agent proposes a rung when money/time pressure is named, never sets one); each rung's legal sheds and the never-bend list live in the economy-ladder section of `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` — every taken shed is named in the delivery report, and an explicit host line outlives any rung | visible |
64	| `far-tier.surface-cadence` | at most once every 14 days — how often the far backlog may surface itself unasked in the status report (SPEC INV-223, roadmap row 403); the report records the last surfacing in a dated marker, and a second offer inside the window is the defect the report-shape check reds | the person's own cadence, moved by his word like any default, and recorded in his profile | internal |
65	
66	The Card column says what the settings card renders. A `visible` row appears on the card. An `internal` row is workshop machinery the card leaves out, reaching the reader only as a recorded host-profile line in the card's project-rules part. The card's own law lives in `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` (INV-87).
67	
68	A profile file is plain markdown: one `setting: value` line per override, each with a trailing date and,
69	when it narrows the defaults, one line saying why. Settings not listed above may be proposed as wishes, and the
70	table grows through the queue like everything else.
71	
72	### A budget moves the pace, and never the standard
73	
74	A rung of the economy ladder sets how fast and how cheaply the work runs. The standard the work is held
75	to stands outside every rung. A check the method calls for runs at whatever the plan costs. A fresh
76	clean-context agent is raised every time the method asks for one. Four such asks are an adversarial
77	review, a cold reading, a release re-prove, and a deep spec-and-architecture audit. Economy is bought
78	from pace, from batching, and from a cheaper tier on mechanical work. It is never bought from a
79	dropped check. The full never-bend list this rule joins lives in the economy-ladder section of
80	`PRODUCT_SPEC.md` (SPEC INV-40, R220). The owner's word, 2026-08-05 at 22:52: quality never suffers,
81	whatever else does. At 22:12 he had named the smaller plan. He asked that a fresh worker the method
82	needs be raised on it all the same.

| `feedback-upstream` | off — the outbound feedback arm is silent; a host switches it on with a recorded profile line (SPEC INV-161, INV-14) | on: on a rare strong reaction the pack offers, with the human's explicit yes, to draft a private upstream note to the pack's authors into `outbox/`; never sends, delivery the human's own step | internal |
| `lanes.cap` | 3 — up to three build lanes roll at once without asking (SPEC T-18, INV-214) | a leaner plan lowers it, a richer one raises it, recorded with the plan it fits; the owner's 2026-07-06 value of three lives in his profile | internal |
| `budget.pressure` | full — every check runs at full strength; the economy ladder's rung (SPEC T-19, INV-40); a rung moves the pace and never the standard, stated under this table | lean or tight, only on the human's word (a session's word or a profile line; asked — or the default told — at a project's setup, founding or adoption, alongside `project.kind`; the agent proposes a rung when money/time pressure is named, never sets one); each rung's legal sheds and the never-bend list live in the economy-ladder section of `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` — every taken shed is named in the delivery report, and an explicit host line outlives any rung | visible |
| `far-tier.surface-cadence` | at most once every 14 days — how often the far backlog may surface itself unasked in the status report (SPEC INV-223, roadmap row 403); the report records the last surfacing in a dated marker, and a second offer inside the window is the defect the report-shape check reds | the person's own cadence, moved by his word like any default, and recorded in his profile | internal |

The Card column says what the settings card renders. A `visible` row appears on the card. An `internal` row is workshop machinery the card leaves out, reaching the reader only as a recorded host-profile line in the card's project-rules part. The card's own law lives in `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` (INV-87).

A profile file is plain markdown: one `setting: value` line per override, each with a trailing date and,
when it narrows the defaults, one line saying why. Settings not listed above may be proposed as wishes, and the
table grows through the queue like everything else.

### A budget moves the pace, and never the standard

A rung of the economy ladder sets how fast and how cheaply the work runs. The standard the work is held
to stands outside every rung. A check the method calls for runs at whatever the plan costs. A fresh
clean-context agent is raised every time the method asks for one. Four such asks are an adversarial
review, a cold reading, a release re-prove, and a deep spec-and-architecture audit. Economy is bought
from pace, from batching, and from a cheaper tier on mechanical work. It is never bought from a
dropped check. The full never-bend list this rule joins lives in the economy-ladder section of
`PRODUCT_SPEC.md` (SPEC INV-40, R220). The owner's word, 2026-08-05 at 22:52: quality never suffers,
whatever else does. At 22:12 he had named the smaller plan. He asked that a fresh worker the method
needs be raised on it all the same.

2	name: build-pipeline
3	description: Use to run a non-trivial feature, bug fix, behavior change, refactor, docs-only change, or feature removal through the full spec-to-ship pipeline. Use it as well to set a project up on live-spec, where it reads the tree, picks the setup walk, and runs it. Spoken: attach live-spec to this project, adopt or install live-spec here, onboard this codebase onto live-spec, found a new project on live-spec, update live-spec here. A tiny reversible edit and pure research stay outside the pipeline.
4	metadata:
5	  version: 5.0.0
6	---
7	
8	# build-pipeline — ship a change by the method
9	
10	> Part of the **live-spec pack** — the shared working rules (ask-never-guess · plain words, anchors trail ·
11	> one surface = one name · one home per fact · junior/senior split · checkpoints · the concurrent-edit
12	> fence · freshness · journal discipline · attic-never-delete · verify by deed · the human's gates · claims
13	> need primary sources · fix the class, sweep look-alikes · the door before code · prototype ≠ product) live ONCE in the pack's base skill, `live-spec-base` (v5.0.0), together with the
14	> settings ladder — this skill references them and elaborates only its own domain. Used standalone, this
15	> note is plain advice.
16	
17	## Words this skill uses
18	
19	**Where the paths point.** Two repositories are in play. A path naming `skills/`, `guardrails/`,
20	`scripts/`, `templates/`, or `tests/` sits in the live-spec pack's own repository,
21	`github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. An install copies each skill folder into one place, so a path
22	naming another skill points to that skill's folder, beside this skill's folder. A path opening with
23	`references/` names a file inside this skill's own directory, beside this file. Every other path
24	belongs to the project under change, including `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`,
25	`TEST_MATRIX.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `JOURNAL.md`, `docs/prover/`, and `.live-spec/`.
26	
27	- **the pack** — the shipped live-spec method: its skills, its document templates, and its gates.
28	  `skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md` holds the shared rulebook and names the ten working skills.
29	- **host** — one project the pack attaches to. Each host holds its own spec, queue, journal, and
30	  `.live-spec/` folder.
31	- **the human** — the person who owns the product decisions. A taste call, a threshold, and a policy
32	  all reach them.
33	- **seat** — the orchestrating session that owns judgment, briefs workers, and reports to the human.
34	  This page also calls that actor the senior and the orchestrator.
35	- **worker** — a delegated session the seat briefs for bounded mechanical work, narrowed to the files
36	  its brief names. This page also calls it the junior.
37	- **wish** — one request as it was spoken, before the door places it.
38	- **door** — the intake classification that places a wish at one entry point: feature, bug, refactor,
39	  docs-only, or skip. It is decided before any code is written, and it stands apart from the wish's size.
40	- **work-kind** — the intake axis naming what a wish produces: product, infra, skill, or prose.
41	- **footprint** — the reach of one change: presentation-only, single-module, or cross-cutting.
42	- **tripwire** — one fixed rule in the door step that lifts a wish to a door whatever its casual label.
43	- **row** — one line of the project's queue, `ROADMAP.md` in this pack, holding one piece of work.
44	- **spec-delta**, also **the delta** — the set of spec sentences one wish adds or changes.
45	- **regression fence** — one sentence in a delta naming a neighbouring promise that must stay true,
46	  citing the existing clause it guards.
47	- **landing** — the act of one piece of work reaching the repository's shared truth as one commit.
48	- **lane**, also **train** — one build lane a session rolls through the pipeline.
49	- **the pen** — the single write-lock a repository holds. One lane at a time writes shared files under it.
50	- **departures board** — the status view read live off the queue's open rows. It names each rolling
51	  lane's step, and whom a waiting lane waits behind.
52	- **red**, used as a verb — a check fails and stops the work at that point. **Green** names a run with
53	  zero failures.
54	- **gate** — a check that must pass before the work proceeds.
55	- **architecture node** — one named unit in `ARCHITECTURE.md`. It carries one responsibility, owns the
56	  spec facts it implements, and pins them to the code.
57	- **seam** — the named boundary between two nodes, stating what crosses it and who owns the format.
58	- **checkpoint** — a saved point of work a session or a worker resumes from, written under `.live-spec/`.
59	- **norm** — an approved prototype frozen as the binding record of a surface's look and feel, kept
60	  under `docs/norms/`.
61	- **problem ledger** — the per-host file `.live-spec/PROBLEMS.md`, recording the workshop's recurring
62	  operational noise.
63	- **class hunt** — the search a confirmed bug drives before it closes. Name the defect abstractly,
64	  find every sibling of that kind, and fix them together.
65	- **compaction** — the station that removes redundancy from a document or from code.
66	- **shopfront** — the public README as the reader-facing front of a repository.
67	- **attic** — the host's append-only archive folder, `attic/`, where a superseded file moves.
68	
69	**The bracket codes.** `INV-`, `T-`, `E-`, `ACT-`, and `M-` codes index requirements in this pack's
70	own `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`. `PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md` maps each code to the criteria that carry it. The word
71	`SPEC` before a code marks that same home and names no separate series. `M-1` is the milestone gate
72	and `M-6` is the push gate. A **base rule N** points at the numbered rule N in
73	`skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md`; its own frontmatter states how many it carries. A **communicator rule N** points into
74	`skills/communicator/SKILL.md`. That file numbers twice: its behaviour rules carry an inline
75	`(rule N)` tag, and its writing-register checklist restarts at 1. This page names which of the two
76	it means each time.
77	Each sentence beside a code states its own
78	rule in full, so a reader holding this page alone can pass the codes over.
79	
80	## The pipeline in one line
81	
82	One pipeline, and steps 1, 2, 5, and 6 each invoke a named skill. The order is **spec → prove → architecture → prove architecture →
83	matrix → test → code → verify → commit & show**. A bug shortcuts to **bug → matrix → test → code** (citing the
84	existing architecture node it lands in). **Skip the pipeline only if ALL hold:** single
85	file · no new state / element / user-visible behaviour · an existing test level already covers the touched
86	fact (still ship a test; the order of test and fix follows test-author's small-fix path — red first by
87	default, and a one-batch fix owes the mechanical red proof). A skip still owes the door step's spec-backed-literal tripwire: does this edit touch a spec-backed literal or clause? A yes routes the docs and the test into the same session as the fix (SPEC INV-104). Anything touching visibility / layout / colour enters at the matrix step minimum.
88	Otherwise don't skip a step — the bugs that pass every test hide in the steps you skipped. (The private playbook repo's PLAYBOOK.md holds
89	the principle behind each step. This skill is its executable projection; keep the two in sync.)
90	
91	**The craft ladder — which craft's standards judge each step (SPEC INV-33).** Each artifact is judged by its
92	own craft's standards: **spec** — a strong product manager (the user's journey, the
93	product's words) · **prove / prove architecture** — the prover's formal-methods reviewer ·
94	**architecture** — a software architect (nodes, seams, one responsibility each) · **matrix** — a QA
95	automation lead deriving coverage · **test** — the same QA engineer writing it · **code** — a senior
96	developer · **verify** — the visitor's own fresh eyes, the builder's own view set aside · **commit & show** — a careful
97	release hand whose reader is the human.
98	
99	The delivery report's step accounting speaks in these standards. The craft each artifact was made under is
100	namable on ask.
101	
102	The craft takes the work-KIND's form (SPEC INV-22, INV-33): on a prose product the code step is worked as
103	a strong writer, on infra as a toolsmith. The ladder names the archetypes, and the kind says what their
104	standards look like in its medium.
105	
106	## When to run it — and where each kind of change enters
107	- **Step zero, before ANY tool call: name the door aloud (SPEC T-12, INV-16; base rule 15) — and the human hears the intake line back as the capture echo: heard · door · name · row · place on the map (communicator rule 12, its capture-echo behaviour rule; SPEC INV-27, INV-37).**
108	  - The intake line states size (a wish too big for its worth is negotiated in SCOPE — cut surfaces or
109	    split into stages, never a time budget or estimate; proposals proceed on the recommended option and
110	    are surfaced, SPEC T-15) · priority · door: feature · bug · refactor · docs-only · skip · work-kind: product · infra · skill ·
111	    prose — what the wish BUILDS, one kind per wish, scaling the FORM of every step it walks (the
112	    work-kind table at [references/work-kind-table.md](references/work-kind-table.md); SPEC T-16, INV-22).
113	
114	    The same line PLACES the wish on the product's feature map — **changes feature X · a new feature ·
115	    restructure** — spoken in the echo and written in the row's `map:` note. The map is the spec's scenario
116	    sections plus the architecture's nodes, never a third document. A restructure verdict queues its OWN row
117	    (refactor door if only structure moves, feature door if behaviour moves too); the re-carve happens only
118	    through the architecture step and its re-prove (SPEC INV-37). A same-version docs-layout pass rides one sanctioned light vehicle: the pass builds on a clean pushed base, locks the owner's decisions in a checkpoint first, and proves content survived by a word-token multiset check and a punctuation multiset check (SPEC INV-111).
119	  - **The same line reads the FOOTPRINT — a three-source impact read that decides the route (SPEC INV-128).**
120	    Beside the door and the work-kind, read the change against three sources at once: the spec (what
121	    behaviour changes), the architecture (which module owns it), the code (what actually gets touched). Name
122	    one footprint — **presentation-only** (touches what the audience meets, nothing behind it) · **single-module**
123	    (stays inside one owned layer) · **cross-cutting** (moves a shared law or several layers) — spoken in the
124	    echo and written in the row's `footprint:` note beside `door:`, `kind:`, `map:`. **The footprint composes
125	    with the door, never overriding it:** the door decides which steps run, the footprint decides how far each
126	    step reaches, and the door's guarantees always hold — a feature never skips the spec step whatever its
127	    footprint (SPEC INV-16). A cross-cutting change opens the full pipeline from step 1, its architecture and
128	    matrix work spanning every layer it moves. A single-module change runs the steps its door grants with their
129	    scope narrowed to the one owned module (its architecture read, its matrix rows, its tests bounded to that
130	    module's block and interface); a single-module bug or refactor takes the existing matrix-step entry, a
131	    single-module feature keeps its spec step with the rest scoped down. A presentation-only change takes the
132	    lightest road its door already grants — the skip boundary or the docs-only door where the door routes it
133	    there, and the matrix-step minimum focused on the visible layer where it is a visible feature. The
134	    footprint sizes the reach, and the wish's size does not — a heavy process on a light change is as much a defect as the
135	    reverse. When the three sources DISAGREE (a spec-promised surface with no owning node, code behaviour no
136	    clause backs, a node pinned to a moved line), name the disagreement and route it to its owner (a bug row, a
137	    spec fix, a restructure row — SPEC INV-37), never silently trusting one source; the three-source read is
138	    the verdict derive-before-fork (SPEC INV-121) rests on. The footprint **re-classifies mid-work** the moment
139	    an edit reaches past its named layer (presentation → single-module, single-module → cross-cutting), the
140	    delivery report recording footprint held or re-classified to X at step N — the sibling of the door's
141	    mid-work re-fire below. (The mechanical `footprint:`-note suite check [INV-134], the per-kind
142	    concrete-layers-and-proofs declaration [INV-135], and the cross-cut counter [INV-128 boundary-health,
143	    `guardrails/crosscut_counter.py`] have landed; the declared-module-interface and interface-level test
144	    machinery rides its own follow-on row; this step states the read and the routing.)
145	  - Tripwires decide by rule, ahead of judgment — a new user-visible surface · new persistent state · a new interaction on an existing surface
146	    · the spec marks the touched surface [target] · behaviour no spec clause backs ⇒ FEATURE, however
147	    casually asked. The tripwire verdict outranks a casual "bugfix" label, and queue-cutting belongs to the
148	    bug door alone — a re-doored wish takes no preemption.
149	  - Re-fire the door mid-work the moment the work is
150	    about to create a surface or state its door doesn't grant: STOP, reclassify, continue by the right
151	    door. When the re-door creates a surface or state that did not exist when the lanes opened, the same
152	    re-check **re-runs the independence edges against every rolling lane (SPEC INV-131)** — the new surface
153	    can collide with a sibling that was independent a moment ago; a new edge pulls the re-doored lane back
154	    to serial (waiting behind the lane it now shares a surface with) with a board line, so the departures
155	    board never asserts a stale independence after the ground moved. The integration re-fence [INV-39]
156	    still catches the collision at landing; this closes the board's observability gap and adds no new net.
157	  - **A declared mockup-first entry condition is honoured from the row, cancelled only by name (SPEC
158	    INV-43).** A story whose intake said "show me first, then build" carries the condition WRITTEN in
159	    its queue row ("entry: mockup-first"); a later general "go build" moves priority, never the
160	    condition — only by the human naming it does the condition fall. A condition living only in chat
161	    memory is the defect this line prevents (the tlvphoto door was built past its voiced mockup-first word).
162	  - **One wish = one user story (SPEC T-17):** a wish carrying several distinct things a person will DO and
163	    SEE splits at intake — each story its own row through the full pipeline (stages slice ONE story's depth,
164	    T-15's knife; separate stories never fuse into one row). Sub-behaviours (a hover face, a phone face, a
165	    backpointer) are the story's ACCEPTANCE, folded into the one story. Unclear whether it is one story or
166	    two ⇒ ask at intake, and every row born of a split cites the one spoken wish it came from. A request to
167	    merely SEE/TRY with no commitment goes to a labelled prototype home instead (base rule 16) — it stays a
168	    prototype, outside prod and unshown as product.
169	- **The door set is CLOSED, and a request enters at the highest document its change reaches (SPEC INV-151).** A request enters at the highest document in the derivation chain — spec → architecture → matrix → code → docs — whose sentences must change to satisfy it; the settings ladder stands beside the chain for a pure value. Walk the chain from the top: after this is done, would any sentence in this document read differently? The first yes is the entry layer, and the request flows down through every step its door grants. The set of entry points is closed — every request kind has a named home and a mandatory back-check, and a request the set cannot place is one plain question, never an improvised route:
170	
171	  See [references/request-kind-table.md](references/request-kind-table.md) for the full closed set of
172	  request kinds, their entry step, and mandatory back-check (product behaviour · a technically-phrased request · a defect · docs-only · a tiny reversible edit · a settings/parameter value · an inbox wish · a method/skill change · a sketch · research/a question · a feedback hand-back).
173	
174	  **A request that matches no kind in this closed set becomes one plain question to the human (base rule 1), never a guessed route.** The closed set is what makes "no gap between the layers" a checkable property held by rule, where before it leaned on habit: the landing contract already lists every door-granted step applied or stood down by name (SPEC INV-22), so a request the set cannot place is surfaced to the human as a question. This is the request-side twin of the property net's homeless-item finding (SPEC INV-150), the deferral test's (SPEC INV-152), and the earned message's (SPEC INV-189, INV-191) — one routing principle stated four times (SPEC INV-153): every incoming thing routes to the home whose declared sentence governs it, and a thing that pins to no home is itself the finding. The fourth control carries it across a window's edge: a message to another agent routes to the sender's own blocked work, and a question no work stands on is dropped and never sent.
175	- **New feature / new stateful surface / behaviour change:** the full pipeline from step 1.
176	- **Bug:** enter at the matrix step with a red-on-bug test (`bug → matrix → test → code`); if the fixed fact
177	  also lives in SPEC prose, update the spec sentence in the same change. **The door step adds one tripwire at the bug door:** does this edit touch a spec-backed literal or clause (a version string, a pinned count, a named vocabulary, a promised wording)? A yes binds the docs-travel-with-the-change rule and the red-first small-fix path into one duty — the docs and the test land in the same session as the fix; the tripwire reads the edit's content, so a one-word change to a spec-cited literal owes the same duty as a full feature (SPEC INV-104). **A confirmed bug drives a class hunt before it closes (SPEC INV-124). The hunt is four moves:** (1) name the defect abstractly (the KIND of mistake — a scope too narrow, a
178	  missing guard, an assumption that holds in one place and fails in the neighbour), then actively SEARCH
179	  every surface where that kind could live and fix all siblings in the same change — the search goes
180	  finding the siblings not yet seen, the matrix row and the red-on-bug test covering the CLASS beyond the
181	  single instance (base rule 14); (2) check the architecture — a structural cause (a boundary drawn wrong
182	  or left silent, a node owning what it should not) updates ARCHITECTURE.md in the same change, a cluster
183	  in one district reading as an architecture smell; (3) check the spec — a spec silent on or
184	  under-describing the broken behaviour is the real defect, fixed FIRST so the prover can flag it, then
185	  the code fix lands under it (the spec-under-describes-composition lesson, generalized); (4) escalate to
186	  the human when the class boundary needs his read — which behaviours are one class, what the intended
187	  design was, whether a whole area wants a rethink — the method stops and asks for the boundary, and does not guess it. The four moves are the bug door's close condition; a point fix that leaves the siblings
188	  standing is a status, never a landing (SPEC INV-26). **A RECURRING bug re-doors to feature:**
189	  a second bug in the same area within ~30 days is not another patch — the area is missing an INVARIANT,
190	  so it escalates to the full pipeline from step 1 (spec the invariant, re-prove, then fix under it).
191	  The journal is how you notice: before taking any bug, grep JOURNAL.md for the area's name and check
192	  the dates.
193	- **Removal of a shipped feature is a change too:** spec section → dated REMOVED tombstone · matrix rows
194	  retired (not left "BUILT") · owning tests deleted · SKILL.md / README swept — all the same session. (This
195	  is the step that actually got skipped once: an excision cleaned code + tests but left four doc surfaces dangling.)
196	- **Refactor (behaviour-neutral):** no spec/matrix delta, but enter at step 8 with the FULL suite + the
197	  visual sample set + a matrix audit of the touched sections (a monolith refactor re-risks everything);
198	  if the refactor moves node boundaries but leaves the document's shape standing, ARCHITECTURE.md's pins
199	  update in the same change — the pins-only path is scoped to a boundary shift that leaves the document's
200	  shape standing. A deliberate redesign (layers restacked, a surface's ownership moved, nodes merged or
201	  split) re-shapes the architecture document to the new form and re-proves it with the architecture lens
202	  in the same movement (SPEC INV-113); updating the pins alone does not cover a redesign.
203	- **Docs-only change:** re-read the changed section rendered + one grep that no stale claim contradicts the
204	  code; no spec/matrix step.
205	- **A rewrite or restyle accounts for every removal of substance (SPEC INV-109):** the rule's one home is communicator rule 6, the removal-accounting step of that skill's writing-register checklist, which owns the delivery report the accounting rides. The docs-only door above and the restyle loop both invoke it — every removed section, argument, rationale, or worked example listed there with its one line of judgment, a removal the rewriter cannot justify raised as a question before the report closes, line-level wording left free.
206	- **A restructure or migration merged back to main is gated on the delta (SPEC INV-114):** A restructure or migration merge gate judges the delta. It has three parts: load-bearing token identity old-versus-new modulo the per-chunk named deltas plus the punctuation-multiset check (SPEC INV-111); the full suite green on the merged tree (SPEC INV-39); and a full prover pass on both sides whose blocking set is delta-scoped — an unmatched token, a red suite, a new-side finding absent on the old side, or an unnamed meaning change. Pre-existing findings equal on both sides route to queue rows in the same landing and never block. And a session that sharpens a human's spoken bar beyond his words says the sharpened form back and marks it as its own interpretation. The token-identity part scopes to a content-preserving restructure. A deliberate redesign changes content by intent, so it routes by the architecture-redesign law (SPEC INV-113), and its merge stands on the green suite and the delta-scoped prover pass, with no token-identity demand over text the redesign meant to change.
207	- **Skip entirely** only under the single boundary above (pure research, fact-gathering, a one-file
208	  no-new-behaviour edit already covered by a test level).
209	
210	## Work that belongs elsewhere
211	
212	Skip it for the skip-boundary edit (single file · no new state, element, or visible behaviour · an existing
213	test level already covers the touched fact — it still ships a test, just no pipeline); not for pure
214	research or fact-gathering (no artifact changes); not for a SEE/TRY ask (that goes to the labelled
215	prototype home, base rule 16 — and comes BACK through this pipeline only at promotion).
216	
217	## Setting a project up on the pack
218	
219	A session that hears "attach live-spec to this project", "found a new project on live-spec", or
220	"update live-spec here" runs a setup walk first. Read
221	[references/project-setup.md](references/project-setup.md), the routing card beside this page. It
222	resolves the pack tree, reads the project tree, and names the walk this project takes. The setup
223	entry stands outside the derivation chain, beside the sketch lane. When the walk finishes, the first wish enters at its
224	own door like any other request.
225	
226	## The work-kind table — WHAT the wish builds scales HOW each step runs (SPEC T-16, INV-22)
227	
228	The door picks WHICH steps run. The kind picks the FORM each running step takes. The work-kind table
229	at [references/work-kind-table.md](references/work-kind-table.md) is the per-kind meanings' one
230	normative home. That is the one place they are stated, and the spec binds the contract around it. The
231	contract, before the table: at landing, every door-granted step has either **APPLIED in its kind's form
232	or STOOD DOWN by name** in the delivery report ("design-sync — text product, stands down") — a silently
233	skipped step is a defect. **An unresolved kind scales nothing down** — standing a step down requires a
234	NAMED kind (the ask rides the row, SPEC INV-12). And no kind ever touches the safety net: the door law
235	and its tripwires, the delta's mandatory sentences (fences · facets · non-goals · success measure),
236	ask-at-intake — the same law a scope cut obeys (SPEC T-15).
237	
238	See [references/work-kind-table.md](references/work-kind-table.md) for the full table of how each step
239	(1 spec · 2 prove · 3 architecture · 4 prove architecture · 5 matrix · 6 test · 7 code · 8 verify by deed · 9 commit & show · design-sync/snapshot) takes shape under product / infra / skill / prose, including the verify-by-deed VISITOR WALK and FEEL pass (SPEC INV-30, INV-136, INV-139) and the skill-review duty (SPEC INV-99).
240	
241	## The steps
242	
243	1. **Spec — invoke `spec-author`.** Write or grow the project `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`: entities, states, transitions,
244	   actors, invariants, and the cross-section composition between surfaces. One surface = one name. Compose
245	   every stateful surface across **every** view/mode axis it lives under, including axes beyond its own. Real gaps are
246	   marked `⟨DECIDE⟩` and asked, never guessed. Use human-first language, with codes at line ends.
247	
248	   A feature-doored wish also walks the **fit walk** — the kind-scaled product-fit interrogation (journey ·
249	   flows · trigger lenses; lens lists live in spec-author; prover mode FEATURE-FIT; SPEC INV-29) — and the
250	   **standard-facet sweep** (the canonical list lives in spec-author): phone/narrow layout · touch-vs-hover ·
251	   empty/error/loading · accessibility · performance. Every facet ends as a spec sentence, decided or

501	## Guardrails — the pipeline's mechanical enforcement (every project inherits them)
502	The nine steps are guidance, and an agent drifts from guidance — that is the failure that stops a project
503	converging (a whole panel ships empty; a behaviour nobody asked for gets buried; a change lands with no test).
504	So the pipeline is not trusted, it is ENFORCED: a `guardrails` check the project wires to a **git pre-push
505	hook** (+ the suite), so a change that fails ANY of these is RED and CANNOT be pushed. `guardrails/` is a
506	directory of check scripts, and the pack ships one runner, `guardrails/pre-push`, that a project installs
507	as its own `.git/hooks/pre-push`. `tests/test_traceability.py`
508	(below) is the first of these — generalise it to the full set. **Each project INSTANTIATES the checks for its
509	own surfaces; the pipeline REQUIRES the check exists and is green.** This is a first-class step, applied across the whole project as a standing part of the method;
510	a per-project patch does not satisfy it. See
511	[references/guardrails-catalog.md](references/guardrails-catalog.md) for the four mechanical guardrails
512	(Completeness incl. cross-surface policy uniformity SPEC INV-125 · Tests-present · Behaviour-traces-to-spec ·
513	Conflicts).
514	**Honest boundary:** guardrails catch STRUCTURAL defects (empty surface, missing test, untraced behaviour,
515	partial artifact, id/naming conflict). They do NOT catch a subtle SEMANTIC bug (is the number right?) — that
516	still needs `product-prover` + a human's eyes. Enforce structure mechanically, and reason about meaning with
517	the prover. Verify-by-deed (step 8) and commit/push (step 9) both run the guardrails first, so guidance and
518	enforcement agree.

537	- **Before a MINOR (0.x.0) bump:** the 3-pass preventive audit — product-prover on the whole spec + a matrix
538	  audit + a surface-composition check, plus the full design review (SPEC INV-141) and the cross-cut counter
539	  (SPEC INV-128, INV-37) and code compaction as a station beside doc compaction (SPEC INV-123). See
540	  [references/minor-bump-gate.md](references/minor-bump-gate.md) for the full gate procedure.
541	- **Compaction runs every pass, above the milestone gate (SPEC INV-164):** the doc- and code-compaction
542	  stations run at every push, above the MINOR gate that once held them alone. Every push is held to the
543	  reached-clean floor by the mechanical gates — the register lint at zero errors, the redundancy gate at
544	  zero open pairs, and the debt cap that only ratchets down (`scripts/spec-debt-cap.json`) — asserted
545	  against the live document by the suite, so no bloat accumulates between milestones. This is the
546	  fix for the spec bloating when compaction ran milestone-only (2026-07-15).
547	- **Process bookkeeping scales to the delta (SPEC INV-61):** the pre-push re-check keeps its rigor and
548	  scales its FORM — a small delta (skill/prose/infra kind, no new surface, no structure change) ships a
549	  three-line SHORT-FORM record (previous records clean · the delta in one line · the verdict). A
550	  surface-sized or structural delta keeps the full walk. Claims batch per declared lane, and the journal
551	  chapter and the resume rewrite come once per landing batch. Never scaled: the law's own text, the
552	  red-first test, the delta's prove, the gates.
553	- **Order is law:** `spec → prove → architecture → prove architecture → matrix → test → code`;
554	  `bug → matrix → test → code`. Never code first and back-fill a spec — and never jump from spec straight
555	  to tests: the two layers between them (architecture, test-spec derivation) are where whole classes of
556	  holes get caught (SPEC E-14/E-15/INV-15).
557	- **A row closes only whole (SPEC INV-26):** where a row carries several legs, its Done-when enumerates
558	  each, and the delivery report may close the row only with EVERY leg met —
559	  half-done is a status, never a landing. An open leg keeps the row in-work, and the resume file's LIVE-STATE restates it at every
560	  supersession, never compresses it away (still open at compaction ⇒ restated in full).
561	- **Trains, one pen (SPEC T-18, INV-39):** one session may roll up to the profile-declared lane cap of
562	  INDEPENDENT build lanes without asking (`lanes.cap`, package default three [E-13]; the owner's
563	  2026-07-06 value three in his profile; one more opens only on the human's asked word, never silently) —
564	  pairwise independent: no true dependency between them and no same-section / same-behaviour collision —
565	  mere co-location in a shared living doc is not an edge. Opening each lane is narrated, and
566	  every train rides the departures board, a waiting lane naming whom it waits behind. Only penless
567	  stages overlap: a later train's code and tests in its own isolated tree (its delta integrates only
568	  under the pen; the disjoint-file road stays within one lane), read-only analysis free.
569	
570	  Every shared-doc edit, the integration, and the closing of a row take the pen one lane at a time — a
571	  pen-stage is never cut mid-edit — and a landing commit carries exactly one row's delta, its gate run
572	  on a tree clean of the other lanes' unfinished work; that same closing commit moves the row from the
573	  queue's body to the month's archive file with its delivery report (the live-body law, SPEC INV-276).
574	  After a landing, waiting lanes re-fence and
575	  re-run their gates on the new truth. Never across sessions, never mid-milestone. A bug takes the pen
576	  at the end of the current pen-stage and parks every rolling lane, each at its own checkpoint,
577	  resuming in landing order.
578	  **Lanes are picked by a graph, never by mood (SPEC INV-49):** at queue-take read the runnable head
579	  and build the mini dependency graph — an edge only on a true dependency (one row needs another's
580	  landed output) or a same-section / same-behaviour collision (the two rewrite one clause or one
581	  behaviour's rule). Mere co-location in a shared living doc draws no edge: the shared living docs
582	  (PRODUCT_SPEC, ARCHITECTURE, TEST_MATRIX) are a convergence point reconciled at integration, never a
583	  serializing surface. Open lanes on a pairwise-independent set up to the cap. Rows that
584	  collide only at integration — co-location included — pre-roll isolated build stages with the landing
585	  order DECLARED at claim (first-declared lands first, the later re-fences). Tiny rows ride serial — parallel pays only when
586	  build stages dominate the pen work — and the chosen set, the order, and a said-aloud "serial by the
587	  graph" are board lines. The same queue-take also re-scans every deferred row's revisit trigger against
588	  the current moment (SPEC INV-129): a time-bound trigger can come true and lapse between two milestone
589	  gates, so the milestone re-scan is not its only reader — a fired trigger returns its row to the runnable
590	  head right then, so a deferred wish never waits on a trigger nobody reads whichever cadence comes first.
591	
592	  **Opening a lane is an act you PERFORM (SPEC INV-214):** once the graph picks a
593	  pairwise-independent set of two or more runnable rows with lanes free under the cap, open each one — do
594	  not fall back to single-file. The act, `scripts/open-lane.sh <row> <slug>` or the same walk by hand:
595	  stage the row→in-work flip in the queue, run the script to fence-check, refuse a lane past the profile
596	  cap (`lanes.cap`, default three), commit that flip alone to main under the pen (the one-row claim
597	  commit), cut `lane/<row>-<slug>` from it into its own worktree under `.claude/worktrees/`, and print the
598	  worker brief stub naming the branch. Then delegate the lane with the Agent tool's `isolation:
599	  "worktree"` option (it carries no gate, usable today), the brief naming the branch its work rides. Going
600	  single-file while independent lanes stand free is a recorded choice: say the "serial by the graph" board
601	  line and name why (the rows collide, the cap is full, the rows are tiny, or a dependency orders them).
602	  That recorded reason is a discipline you hold, since no gate can judge whether two rows were independent
603	  and owed a parallel lane — that judgment is the graph itself, a senior read (SPEC INV-49, INV-214).
604	
605	  **The drafter-applier pipeline is the standard colliding-rows form (SPEC INV-49):** on colliding rows
606	  the penless DRAFT stage overlaps the current landing, a drafter worker preparing the next row's exact
607	  edit strings while the applier lands the current row under the pen. See
608	  [references/drafter-applier-example.md](references/drafter-applier-example.md) for the drafter's
609	  self-verify list and the 2026-07-12 worked run [T-18, INV-39, INV-49].
610	- **Junior delegation (decided from the request, BEFORE the first tool call, SPEC INV-69):** judgment work
611	  (spec, prove, architecture, matrix-level calls, findings triage, any taste call) stays senior; mechanical
612	  work (known edit strings, a known command, fan-out fact-gathering, a report or list or dump to produce)
613	  routes to a worker at the cheapest tier that can pass the brief, proposed and logged, the senior free to
614	  override aloud. The brief is self-contained (the BMAD story-file lesson) and SIZED, born from reading the
615	  touched files in full with three recorded lines per file — current state, what changes, and what must
616	  survive (SPEC INV-53/54/55) — and closes on a HALT list,
617	  so the worker halts at ambiguity and never guesses past it. The worker contract (SPEC ACT-3) narrows write-ownership to the
618	  brief's named files; the senior owns write-set disjointness between concurrent same-session workers before
619	  spawning them, or gives one an isolated worktree (SPEC INV-105). The brief carries the problem-ledger path
620	  for workshop noise (SPEC INV-23) and the clock for every stamp (SPEC INV-24). And the brief carries the
621	  cleanup-safety constraint: a cleanup acts only on what the run provably owns, targeted by a recorded
622	  process group or an owned install path (SPEC INV-162, base rule 17). Every delegation reports its saving
623	  in the row's delivery report, checked by suite and moved to the archive with the row by the closing
624	  commit (SPEC INV-103, INV-276), and names the reads dispatched beside the work delegated (SPEC INV-137).
625	  See [references/delegation-protocol.md](references/delegation-protocol.md) for the full protocol: the
626	  routing rule, the brief's three birth laws, the worker contract, and the delegation-reporting duty.
627	  Each work block in the report opens by naming its root. The root is the person's dated request, a
628	  standing instruction, or a stated reason, and machinery is never a root. The report accounts each
629	  block against its announced plan line (SPEC INV-314).
630	- **A worker never restores a working tree with a git command (SPEC INV-298; the gate INV-299).** Every
631	  brief this skill composes carries this clause verbatim. Before a worker mutates a file it means to put
632	  back, it reads that file and holds its bytes. A worker puts a file back by WRITING ITS OWN SAVED BYTES.
633	  A worker runs no command that discards uncommitted work, in any tree: `git checkout -- <path>`,
634	  `git checkout .`, `git restore` outside `--staged`, `git stash` and its `push`, `save`, `create` and
635	  `store` forms, `git reset` with `--hard`, `--merge` or `--keep`, and `git clean` with `-f` or `-x`. Such
636	  a command's blast radius is a PATH, so its damage lands on files the worker never wrote and its brief
637	  never named. This rule binds a worker in every tree, including its own isolated worktree, since a
638	  worktree shares one repository with the lanes beside it and a worker cannot read off its brief what else
639	  that repository holds. A worker that holds no saved bytes for a file it mutated, or that believes a file
640	  needs a git-level restore, HALTS and reports the file and the mutation it made, and it writes no further
641	  file and runs no further command. The orchestrator owns recovery: it restores the named file from the
642	  last committed stage, hands the worker a fresh brief carrying that file's current bytes, and records the
643	  halt in the row's delivery report, and the halted work resumes under that new brief. The orchestrator's
644	  own half: a finished build stage is committed before the next worker touches its files.
645	  `guardrails/check-worker-restore.py` reads the worker runs' transcripts for the command and runs at the
646	  verify step.
647	- **Traceability is a test, enforced automatically.** A standing `tests/test_traceability.py` fails the suite on a matrix row
648	  citing a missing test, a duplicate invariant id, a spec invariant with no matrix row, or a ⟨DECIDE⟩ marked
649	  RESOLVED that still carries the live marker — so drift is caught every commit, continuously, and never waits for the next MINOR.
650	
651	## How it relates to the other skills
652	- `spec-author` — writes/grows the spec (step 1). Public.
653	- `product-prover` — reviews the whole spec with formal-verification thinking (step 2). External skill, installed by `scripts/install-external-skills.sh`; pack bindings in `skills/product-prover-pack/SKILL.md`.
654	- `design-reviewer` — a second pass right after the prover (step 2): judges the design, proposes the
655	  same-kind groupings the text never declared, and echoes the strongest likely divergence to the human;
656	  recommendations and questions only, never a block. Public.
657	- `test-author` — derives the matrix and writes the tests (steps 5–6). Public.
658	- `build-pipeline` (this) — the orchestrator that sequences them through to a shipped, verified, committed
659	  change.
660	
661	The pack holds six more skills, and `skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md` names the ten working ones:
662	
663	- `live-spec-base` — the shared rulebook and the settings ladder. Every `base rule N` on this page
664	  points there.
665	- `communicator` — carries the work to the human. Every `communicator rule N` on this page points there.
666	- `publish` — runs the checks a publication owes its reader, invoked at step 9's shopfront walk.
667	- `text-audit` — reads a text as a stranger and repairs where they stop.
668	- `feedback-intake` — files what comes back from a person or an inbox.
669	- `feedback-collector` — offers a rare private note up to the pack's authors.
670	
671	> The method, made durable: spec-author and product-prover each own one step; build-pipeline is the spine that
672	> runs the whole arc from a spec to a shipped, tested, committed change.
673
