content.content:
1	---
2	name: live-spec-base
3	description: Load before using any live-spec pack skill (spec-author, product-prover, design-reviewer, build-pipeline, test-author, communicator, feedback-intake, feedback-collector, text-audit, publish), before briefing a worker that will write files, or to resolve shared rules and settings. It is the one home for the shared rules — thirty-four rules in the body — and for the settings ladder, which sits in `references/settings-ladder.md` and is opened when a setting is being resolved.
4	metadata:
5	  version: 5.0.0
6	---
7	
8	# live-spec-base — one rulebook, ten working skills
9	
10	The pack's shared working rules live here, once. A working skill opens by naming this base and the
11	version it was written against. It then references these rules and elaborates only its own domain.
12	The ten working skills are named in the closing roster below. A second full statement of a shared
13	rule inside a working skill is drift (SPEC INV-13). It is a defect to fold at the next milestone,
14	never kept for convenience. One rule is carried whole instead by every skill that briefs a worker.
15	The worker-restore sub-rule under rule 7 rides each brief in one wording. `tests/test_worker_restore.py`
16	reds a home that states it in words of its own (SPEC INV-299). Communicator teaches how to speak
17	plainly; that we speak plainly is this file's sentence. Used standalone, outside the pack, a
18	working skill still stands: its pointer here reads as plain advice.
19	
20	## Where the paths and the codes in this file point
21	
22	This file names paths of two kinds, resolving in two different trees.
23	
24	**The pack's own machinery** sits in the live-spec repository, whose public home is
25	`github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. Its directories are `guardrails/`, `scripts/`, `tests/`,
26	`templates/`, `hooks/`, `adopt/`, and `skills/`. Each of the ten working skills this file names sits
27	at `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, beside this one. A path beginning `references/` names a file inside this
28	skill's own directory, beside this file, opened on demand at the step that names it.
29	
30	**A host's own documents and workspace** sit at the root of whatever project the pack is attached to.
31	Those are `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `JOURNAL.md`, `NEXT_STEPS.md`,
32	`DECISIONS.md`, `attic/`, `prototype/`, `inbox/`, `outbox/`, `docs/`, and `.live-spec/`. The live-spec
33	repository is a host of its own, so on that one machine the two trees are the same directory.
34	
35	A bracket code such as `INV-4` is a short handle for one rule of the product spec. Its home is
36	`PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, where the code trails the line it names. That file's preamble names every letter a
37	code can carry and what each stands for, so a code this page never uses decodes there. A roadmap row number, such as row 416, names a line of `ROADMAP.md`. A row that has closed
38	rotates to a dated file under `docs/queue-archive/`. So a row cited here may sit there instead. Two
39	other bracket marks read as part of the sentence they sit in, and `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` states both.
40	`[target]` marks a feature or leg that is promised and not yet built. `[default]` names a value the
41	agent set that the person may retune.
42	
43	## The words this file uses
44	
45	Each term is defined once. Most sit in the glossary of `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, whose entry is the authority
46	behind the short read given here.
47	
48	- **the pack** — the shipped live-spec method: its skills, its document and suite templates, and its
49	  guardrail scripts. It carries a version.
50	- **a host** — one project the pack attaches to. Each host holds its own spec, queue, journal, and
51	  `.live-spec/` folder.
52	- **the seat** — the one acting orchestrator session that owns judgment, orchestrates the pipeline,
53	  briefs workers, judges lane independence, and reports to the person. The glossary keeps the one name
54	  seat throughout. It records the senior and the orchestrator as the source's other names for it, and
55	  this file adds a fourth, the lead. The four names mean the one session.
56	- **a worker** — a delegated agent session the seat briefs for a bounded piece of mechanical work,
57	  narrowed to the files its brief names.
58	- **a tier** — the model level a unit of work runs at: a no-decision one-shot worker, a multi-step
59	  mechanical worker, or the seat for judgment. Rule 5 names haiku and sonnet as the two worker levels.
60	- **a brief** — the written instruction set a worker runs from, carrying its files, its steps, its
61	  clock, and its stop conditions.
62	- **a wish** — one request a person voices in plain words, captured as a queue row and carried to a
63	  recorded terminal state.
64	- **a queue row** — one live wish written as exactly five cells of `ROADMAP.md`: its id, the wish,
65	  its class, its status, and its acceptance. Its home is `docs/roadmap-format.md`. This file calls it
66	  a row.
67	- **a lane** — one build train a session rolls through the pipeline. A lane branch is that lane's
68	  isolated copy, a git worktree holding a branch named for its queue row.
69	- **the pen** — the single write-lock a repository holds, under which one delivery reaches the
70	  repository's shared truth at a time.
71	- **a landing** — the act of one piece of work reaching the repository's shared truth as one commit
72	  under the pen.
73	- **a gate** — a check that must pass before work proceeds, and a red gate stops the work at that
74	  step. Where a sentence here says a check *reds* something, it means the check fails on it.
75	- **a checkpoint** — a saved point of work that can be resumed from, written under `.live-spec/`.
76	- **the attic** — the host's append-only archive folder `attic/`. A superseded file moves here with
77	  one manifest line and is kept for good.
78	- **a breakpoint** — a point where a movement ends and session memory can be wiped with no loss, its
79	  live state replaced, a dated journal entry added, and the work committed.
80	- **a door** — the intake classification placing a queued wish at one entry point of the pipeline,
81	  one of feature, bug, refactor, docs-only, or skip. An ask merely to see or try a thing takes a
82	  separate entry lane, the labelled-sketch door, held outside that five-way set.
83	- **an agent** — defined where the rule that binds it stands, at rule 31.
84	- **an agent card** — a host's self-describing file `.live-spec/agent.md`, stating its name, mission,
85	  zones, published contracts, and inbox address. `templates/agent.template.md` gives its shape.
86	
87	## The rule of thinking, above all the rest
88	
89	**Every incoming item is a symptom, and the answer owed is a rule about its class.** One phrase, one
90	file, one number, one incident — whatever arrives, it arrived as an instance of something. Name the
91	class, state the rule for it, find the other live instances, and the instance that was pointed at is
92	repaired as a free consequence. A change that repairs only the instance has answered nothing, because
93	the next instance is already on its way. The rule holds at every channel an item arrives through, and
94	there are three: a person's feedback, a finding the agent makes itself, and a message from another
95	agent. The three are one filter.
96	
97	This is a rule of thinking, and it governs every rule below it. Rule 14 is its mechanism inside a code
98	change. Rule 14 came first because the class-shaped answer was noticed in code, and the thinking
99	generalizes it to everything.
100	
101	Its own worked failure: the guard holding this pack's register laws was built as a list of literal
102	patterns. There was one pattern per phrase someone once caught. So the guard built to enforce the
103	rules was itself the clearest breach of this one. Each caught escape only added one more pattern,
104	while the next new phrasing passed through untouched (proven by probe, 2026-07-17). The repair
105	shipped that day as roadmap row 416, which now sits in
106	`docs/queue-archive/rotated-ROADMAP-2026-07.md`. A law naming a class is held by a judge that reads
107	meaning. If the answer to a class is a list, the design is wrong.
108	
109	## The shared rules
110	
111	Rule 30 was cut whole from this rulebook; its number is retired and stays open. Every other rule below
112	keeps the number it already carries.
113	
114	1. **Ask, never guess.** A gap only the human can fill — a threshold, a policy, a taste call — is asked or
115	   marked `⟨DECIDE⟩` with a one-line question and a recommended pick. Never invent intent, and never ask
116	   what you can decide or verify yourself. A pending question rides in its row while the lane keeps moving
117	   on the recommendation (SPEC INV-4, INV-5, INV-12). And before offering the human a fork, check whether
118	   a proven artifact already settles it. Where the architecture, the spec, or the invariants determine
119	   the answer, derive the requirement. Say it back with the section cited as its ground, offering no fork.
120	   A fork reaches the human only for what the artifacts leave genuinely open (rule 27 names those cases).
121	   This is the read-the-doc twin of ask-never-guess: that half forbids inventing an answer, this half
122	   forbids offering a choice the documents have already made (SPEC INV-121).
123	
124	2. **Plain words carry the meaning; the code trails, quietly.** Every human-facing sentence stands on its
125	   own in the product's language. Internal handles never do the talking: an `INV-x` code, a row number, a
126	   worker name, a model name, a coined feature name, or a metaphor the reader never chose to learn.
127	   One convention, two faces: in **chat**, the anchor may trail the sentence in parentheses —
128	   "no remote copy exists (INV-8)"; in **documents**, anchors sit at line ends in square brackets — `[INV-8]`.
129	   Never open a line with a code. And when chat runs in one language while the docs run in another, a term
130	   or metaphor coined in the docs language is never loan-translated into chat. That is the **no calques**
131	   rule: say what actually happens in natural chat-language words. The original term is free to trail in parentheses like any
132	   anchor. (2026-07-05 — a calque reads as machine-speak and degrades the product.)
133	
134	3. **One surface = one name, everywhere.** The moment one thing answers to two names, every cross-check
135	   silently loses the seam between them. The vocabulary comes from the host's SPEC.
136	
137	4. **One canonical home per fact.** Everything else that mentions the fact is a pointer, and pointers are
138	   kept live — a doc superseded or moved gets every inbound reference repointed the same session. Two
139	   documents claiming authority over one fact is undefined behaviour when they disagree.
140	
141	5. **The lead orchestrates; each unit routes to the cheapest tier that passes its brief (SPEC INV-69).**
142	   The lead — the orchestrator seat, whatever tier holds it — orchestrates, briefs, and accepts the work,
143	   and it does not do the grunt itself. Every unit of work is routed PER UNIT:
144	   the trigger is judgment against mechanical, and the tier is proposed for that unit. A one-shot with no
145	   decision goes to haiku, multi-step mechanical work to sonnet, and anything carrying judgment or design
146	   to the senior, and a judgment step is never routed down. Size is a weak hint only, never the decider.
147	   The worker pastes raw output (command + exit code + failing lines) as it works. Only raw output is
148	   evidence, and the worker's prose is only a lead. So a worker's green is a lead the lead ACCEPTS by
149	   re-checking it, never on trust. A
150	   large or high-stakes landing earns an independent fresh-context checker beyond that re-check (SPEC
151	   INV-46). Every override of a proposed tier and every
152	   failed-acceptance escalation is logged, proposed tier → chosen tier → why (SPEC INV-69).
153	
154	6. **Every long or delegated piece of work keeps a persistent checkpoint.** A file on disk (host home:
155	   `.live-spec/checkpoints/`, gitignored and kept inside the repo tree) holds done / in-progress / next,
156	   updated as the work runs, so a cut-off resumes from disk. A landing that ships a checkpoint's items flips that checkpoint to its closed state in the same
157	   landing, so a returning session never reopens finished work. A checkpoint whose items all live in git
158	   history is stale by definition and reads as a resume defect (SPEC INV-107). Red at a pause is never
159	   committed. The failing test name and the hypothesis become the top item of `NEXT_STEPS.md`, so the
160	   red test is itself the checkpoint. A checkpoint or handoff note that records a live background
161	   worker also records three things about it. First, the worker's id, pointing at the worker's own
162	   checkpoint file. Second, its briefed write-set. Third, the liveness checks a resuming session runs
163	   before touching those files or spawning a sibling. Those checks are the write-set's file times
164	   watched over a short window, the worker's heartbeat, and one message to its id. The heartbeat is a
165	   fixed-interval touch on the worker's own checkpoint file, ~60 s [default],
166	   stale past ~2 min [default]. Such a note never frames the worker's output as finished while the
167	   worker may still run (SPEC INV-76). Before a memory wipe, prefer
168	   halting the workers or letting them finish, so the next session starts single-writer. Say plainly
169	   when a worker dies with a closed window or a sleeping machine. The human's leave-word fires this rule
170	   for everything open at once. Every lane goes to its checkpoint, workers are halted or landed, and green
171	   is committed. One closing line follows, only when the whole walk holds (SPEC INV-95; the communicator
172	   carries the walk).
173	
174	7. **The concurrent-edit fence, before every write and every commit.** Re-check `git status` and HEAD
175	   against what you last read. If HEAD moved, or the tree holds changes you did not make, stop, re-read,
176	   then proceed surgically or back off. A repo you were not assigned to is read-only, apart from a new wish
177	   file in its inbox. This binds every skill that writes shared files, adoption among them (SPEC INV-10,
178	   INV-11).
179	
180	   The parallel-lanes rules sit underneath the fence.
181	   - **Lanes under one pen, up to the profile cap.** Within one session, build lanes roll without asking up
182	     to the profile-declared lane cap (SPEC T-18; `lanes.cap`, package default three [E-13]). One more
183	     opens only on the human's asked word. Every write to a document the lanes share serializes under the
184	     single PEN, one lane at a time. That document is a convergence point the pen reconciles at
185	     integration, so sharing it never makes the lanes wait on each other. Co-location alone never pulls two rows into one lane (SPEC INV-49).
186	   - **The lane-open act.** The session opens a lane by running `scripts/open-lane.sh`, or by walking the
187	     same steps by hand. The script's own header states what it expects on disk. First, the row→in-work flip is committed to main under the pen. Second, the branch
188	     `lane/<row>-<slug>` is cut from that claim commit into its own worktree. Third, the lane goes to a
189	     worker whose brief names the branch. The act reads the profile cap [E-13] and refuses a lane past it.
190	     It runs whenever the dependency graph shows two or more independent runnable rows and lanes stand free.
191	     Going single-file then is recorded on the departures board, the status-report view, as a "serial by the
192	     graph" board reason. Judging independence is a senior read no gate can settle, so this stays a
193	     discipline the session holds (SPEC INV-214, INV-49).
194	   - **Worktree isolation on overlap.** A later lane's code and tests live in its own isolated copy of the
195	     tree until the senior integrates them. So worktree isolation is the default when two lanes' write-sets
196	     overlap. A shared file one lane holds open is never written by another (SPEC INV-105).
197	   - **Brief-time disjointness** — before spawning another concurrent writer, the senior confirms its
198	     brief's write-set is disjoint from every already-running writer's brief, or gives it an isolated
199	     worktree at brief-time. The fence stays silent between same-session siblings and cannot catch the
200	     senior's own workers colliding (SPEC ACT-3, INV-11).
201	   - **A worker never restores a working tree with a git command (SPEC INV-298).** Before a worker mutates a file it means to put back, it reads that file and holds its bytes. A worker puts a file back by WRITING ITS OWN SAVED BYTES. A worker runs no command that discards uncommitted work, in any tree: `git checkout -- <path>`, `git checkout .`, `git restore` outside `--staged`, `git stash` and its `push`, `save`, `create` and `store` forms, `git reset` with `--hard`, `--merge` or `--keep`, and `git clean` with `-f` or `-x`. Such a command's blast radius is a PATH, so its damage lands on files the worker never wrote and its brief never named. This rule binds a worker in every tree, including its own isolated worktree, since a worktree shares one repository with the lanes beside it and a worker cannot read off its brief what else that repository holds. A worker that holds no saved bytes for a file it mutated, or that believes a file needs a git-level restore, HALTS and reports the file and the mutation it made, and it writes no further file and runs no further command. The orchestrator owns recovery: it restores the named file from the last committed stage, hands the worker a fresh brief carrying that file's current bytes, and records the halt in the row's delivery report, and the halted work resumes under that new brief. The orchestrator's own half: a finished build stage is committed before the next worker touches its files. `guardrails/check-worker-restore.py` reads the worker runs' transcripts for the command and runs at the verify step.
202	   - **One row per landing commit.** A landing commit carries exactly one row's delta (SPEC INV-39). Its
203	     gate runs on a tree clean of any other lane's unfinished work.
204	   - **A prior-context worker.** A background worker from a prior context is a concurrent writer too. It
205	     survives a memory wipe, and the process list and the harness task panel are never proof of death. It
206	     stays a foreign writer until verified by rule 6's three resume checks. No second worker goes onto a
207	     shared tree until the first replies that it halted, or all three checks declare it dead. The fence's
208	     silence between same-session siblings never crosses the wipe (SPEC INV-76).
209	   - **A stable session identity breaks the pen tie.** Every session mints a stable identity at its start
210	     and records it in its `.live-spec/` checkpoint, unchanged for its life. The identity is the harness
211	     session id where the context carries one. Otherwise it is the start time joined with the worktree path
212	     and a single-use random string. On a genuine concurrent claim with no git ancestry, the pen tie-break
213	     orders on this identity, so exactly one session backs off (SPEC INV-117).
214	
215	8. **Freshness: versions are re-checked at every breakpoint.** Read the modification time of the
216	   installed skills, the pack, and the profiles. On any version change, re-read the changed file before
217	   continuing, work only from that freshly read copy, and journal one line naming old → new (SPEC A-7,
218	   M-7).
219	
220	9. **History lives in the journal; docs travel with the change.** The dated reason behind every movement
221	   goes to `JOURNAL.md` the same session. The prose of `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, `NEXT_STEPS.md`, and

553	     message's carrier while leaving its authority where it started [INV-193].
554	
555	32. **A release's number answers what taking it costs a host (SPEC INV-217).** The number reports what a
556	   host that vendored the previous version must do to take this one. A **patch** fixes a machine to hold a
557	   law already stated: no new capability, no changed contract, and the host takes it and does nothing. A
558	   **minor** grows what a host may adopt in a backward-compatible way: a new capability, a new law, or a
559	   new gate. The host takes it by re-running its catch-up walk [INV-91], with nothing it already carries
560	   rewritten. A **major** is a release a host cannot take without changing what it already carries. Four
561	   things earn it: a reworded rule the host vendored, a renamed or removed surface a host depends on, a
562	   changed adoption or catch-up step, a moved law that forces host action. A major ships its dated
563	   `MIGRATION.md` chapter [INV-91]. The default is a patch. It is raised to a minor or a major only where
564	   the release earns the higher tier. This is a judgment the releasing session makes and states, **held by
565	   no machine**. The minor-versus-major call reads meaning a gate cannot, so it **stays a stated rule the
566	   session holds**, the same standing as a design-review finding that never blocks a lane [INV-141]. The
567	   2.0.0 release is the boundary case. Its migration chapter records "Host action: none", so by this rule
568	   it reads as a minor. It keeps its published number as this cited boundary case.
569	
570	33. **The authoring seat does not adversarially certify its own work (SPEC INV-237).** The seat that
571	   authored a change drafts and accepts it, and it never provides that change's own adversarial
572	   certification. A head marinated in the authoring context is blind to the blind spot it just wrote. Two
573	   carriers hold it. A release's adversarial pass — the full re-prove at the release gate [INV-116] — is
574	   authored by a fresh seat. That seat is a differently-contexted head briefed from the primary sources.
575	   It is the same freshness the verify audit already demands of its checker (SPEC INV-46).
576	   The 2.7.0 release ran its adversarial pass
577	   in the context that authored the new lenses, and so
578	   never turned a brand-new lens onto the skill body that introduced it. And a newly added lens or rule is
579	   run against the very document that introduces it before release, which is self-application, with the
580	   release record
581	   naming the result. A release gate may require a dated clean-context review record naming a seat other
582	   than the release's. Whether the review was truly clean-context is a process fact no gate fully sees.
583	   So the gate checks only that the record exists, is dated to the release, and names a different seat.
584	   That is the mechanical floor under a discipline the seat holds. The owner's word, 2026-07-18, after a fresh web
585	   review caught self-referential defects the in-context 2.7.0 prover missed.
586	
587	34. **A deferred item's own state is re-derived from the code before its work resumes (SPEC INV-247).** A
588	   resume file and a queue row record a past moment. The technical problem statement a deferred or
589	   queued item carries — how the code it touches works — can go stale as that code moves on. So the first
590	   act of resuming such an item is a freshness check of its own subject against the shipped source. Read
591	   the code the item touches, confirm the problem the row describes still holds, and re-derive the item's
592	   real current state before designing anything on it. It is the resume-side twin of rule 13's primary
593	   source and of the architecture step's pin read from a command just run. Rule 8 re-reads versions at a
594	   breakpoint, and the queue-take re-scan re-reads a deferred row's revisit trigger [SPEC INV-129].
595	   This rule re-reads the item's own internals. So
596	   a session never designs a fix from a stale model of code that has since moved, and an item already handled
597	   is caught before the work restarts. The owner asked the pack to hold it, 2026-07-20.
598	
599	35. **A session's record is read at both ends by an agent that did not live it (SPEC INV-302).** A session
600	   that lived the work reads its own record badly. Worked failure: on 2026-07-28 a session wrote its
601	   handover from memory. It named a question as still waiting for the owner, and the owner had answered
602	   it earlier that day. So each
603	   end of a session is read by a fresh agent. That agent works from a session extract: the person's own
604	   turns, each with its timestamp. `scripts/session-extract.py` pulls those turns out of one transcript,
605	   and its own header names where the transcripts sit and which traps a reader meets there.
606	   The extract goes to a scratch directory, since a transcript holds private conversation. At the close,
607	   the fresh agent writes the session handover from that extract. The session that lived the work writes
608	   no handover of its own. A handover is a file under `docs/handovers/` whose name ends in
609	   `-handover.md`, and it says where it was read from in three lines: transcript, extract, written by.
610	   At the open, a fresh agent reads the previous session's extract. It lists every decision the person
611	   made, each with its timestamp. It compares that list against `DECISIONS.md` and `NEXT_STEPS.md`. A
612	   decision missing from both goes to the seat before work starts.
613	   Both ends stay a discipline the seat holds. A script read the handover's three lines until
614	   2026-08-09, and the live-spec pack withdrew that script after finding no error the script had
615	   ever caught.
616	   A session's opening writes no committed artifact for a script to read. The owner asked for
617	   this reading as a standing process, 2026-07-28.
618	
619	
620	## Work that belongs elsewhere
621	
622	Reserve this file for the pack's own work: a session outside the pack uses a general style guide instead.
623	Never write host- or person-specific values here — those live in profiles, and this file holds only
624	package defaults and the rules themselves. The scope is pack-internal by the owner's decision (recorded
625	2026-07-16). The base serves the pack's skills and the projects that adopted the pack. It is no
626	general-purpose rulebook for unrelated sessions. That decided sentence closes the recurring scope
627	question for good.
628	
629	## The settings ladder
630	
631	How the pack behaves is a **named setting** in one of four nested scopes. Resolution reads from the
632	narrowest scope out — **session beats host beats personal beats package default** (SPEC E-13).
633	
634	The ladder itself is one module in this same package:
635	[references/settings-ladder.md](references/settings-ladder.md), beside this file. It holds the four
636	scopes and their homes. It holds the package-defaults table every setting is a row of. It holds the
637	rule that a budget moves the pace and never the standard.
638	
639	Open that module when a setting is being resolved, proposed, or recorded, and not before. Nothing in
640	it is optional. Nothing in it moved elsewhere: the module is the ladder's one home, read on demand
641	rather than carried by every session that touches no setting.
642	
643	> The pack, whole: **live-spec-base** holds the shared rules and defaults · **spec-author** writes the spec ·
644	> **product-prover** reviews it · **product-prover-pack** binds the external prover to the pack · **design-reviewer** judges the design behind it · **build-pipeline** ships the change · **test-author** derives the matrix and writes the tests · **communicator** makes the human
645	> exchange land · **feedback-intake** brings what comes back to its home · **feedback-collector** offers a rare private note up to the authors · **text-audit** reads a text as a stranger and fixes where they stop · **publish** sees the work out the door, owing its kind's checklist.
646

---
name: live-spec-base
description: Load before using any live-spec pack skill (spec-author, product-prover, design-reviewer, build-pipeline, test-author, communicator, feedback-intake, feedback-collector, text-audit, publish), before briefing a worker that will write files, or to resolve shared rules and settings. It is the one home for the shared rules — thirty-four rules in the body — and for the settings ladder, which sits in `references/settings-ladder.md` and is opened when a setting is being resolved.
metadata:
  version: 5.0.0
